Why only 11 episodes from 25 presses

25 keypresses total: 14 stops and 11 resumes. Split by session — 111808 gave 5 stops + 4 resumes, 112310 gave 6 + 5, 113316 gave 3 + 2.

A detectable episode needs a resume to start the clock and a stop to score against. The first stop in each session has no preceding resume, so those three are unusable. 14 − 3 = 11. That is the entire training and test set, and it is thin — worth remembering before reading much into any single number below.

The HR trigger fires systematically early

Your read of the first report is correct, and it holds up when each channel is run on its own rather than racing them:

ChannelnMean ΔMedianSDLate firesRange
Girth8−2.51 s−1.87 s3.49 s3−7.8 … +3.4
Heart rate3−7.86 s−8.29 s3.04 s0−11.3 … −3.9

The gap is about 5.4 s and the mechanism is visible in episode 02: heart rate reaches its ceiling and goes flat — first derivative pinned at exactly zero — several seconds before girth stops climbing. A rollover detector on HR therefore has to fire earlier. It is not noise; HR simply saturates first.

But HR is not just noise to be suppressed. In episodes 07 and 09 girth's rollover came after the press (+2.7 s and +0.6 s) and HR was the only channel that fired in time. Removing HR turns 1 late fire into 3.

Three ways to use that

StrategyLateMean ΔSDMedian |Δ|
Either channel, whichever first1−3.97 s4.133.94 s
Girth only3−2.09 s3.632.66 s
Girth, HR delayed +3 s1−3.15 s3.533.41 s

Delaying the HR trigger by 3 s keeps both rescues and removes most of the over-earliness. Raising the HR threshold instead does nothing useful — HR's rollover is so clean that any threshold it clears at all, it clears early.

The honest caveat: this offset is fitted on three HR fires. It is a plausible correction, not a validated one.

How to read the panels

Each episode gets six panels — girth on the left, heart rate on the right; value, first derivative, second derivative going down. Time is relative to the actual press, so zero is where you hit space. The bold line is the 1.5 s causal span the detector uses; the faint line behind it is a 3 s span, there to show the trend through the noise.

Everything is causal — trailing windows only — so what you see at any x is what the detector knew at that moment, nothing from the future.

actual press resume girth trigger HR trigger

Two artefacts worth knowing before you go hunting: the HR sensor reports integer bpm at ~2.7 Hz, so its trace is quantised into steps and its derivative sits at exactly zero across each step. Girth samples at ~8.9 Hz and is genuinely continuous. Second derivatives on HR are therefore much less trustworthy than on girth.

The eleven episodes

01 · 111808 resume @80.4s · on-time 15.8s

girth -7.1 s HR -3.3 s

Girth velocity is strongly multi-peaked — three separate crests. The trigger takes the first sustained rollover, which is why it lands 7.1 s out. HR has already flattened by then.

02 · 111808 resume @115.4s · on-time 16.3s

girth -7.8 s HR -2.8 s

HR reaches 80 bpm at −5 s and holds it flat to the press; its derivative sits at exactly zero. Girth is still climbing. This is the clearest example of HR saturating before girth does.

03 · 111808 resume @152.4s · on-time 6.8s

girth -0.5 s HR +3.5 s

A short, clean episode. Both channels rise monotonically and girth rolls over almost exactly on the press. HR overshoots into late territory.

04 · 111808 resume @200.6s · on-time 5.9s

girth -2.0 s HR +10.7 s

Girth flattens at −2 s and the trigger catches it. HR is still rising steeply at the press and does not roll over until +10.7 s — HR is useless here.

05 · 112310 resume @50.4s · on-time 9.6s

girth -4.3 s HR +1.3 s

Girth's steepest episode (peak velocity 150 counts/s). Sharp rise, sharp rollover, fires 4.3 s early. HR lags behind and fires late.

06 · 112310 resume @90.9s · on-time 3.7s

girth +3.4 s HR +8.3 s

The 3.7 s episode. Both channels are still accelerating when the press happens — the second derivative is positive on both. Nothing has rolled over; both triggers are late by construction.

07 · 112310 resume @124.6s · on-time 7.9s

girth +2.7 s HR -3.9 s

Girth's rollover is shallow and late (+2.7 s); HR's is clean and early (−3.9 s). One of the two cases where HR genuinely rescues the decision.

08 · 112310 resume @172.4s · on-time 4.3s

girth -0.1 s HR +6.6 s

Very short episode, girth catches it at −0.1 s almost by luck. HR is 6.6 s late.

09 · 112310 resume @207.0s · on-time 14.6s

girth +0.6 s HR -8.3 s

Long episode. Girth plateaus then resumes climbing, so its rollover is late (+0.6 s). HR fires 8.3 s early. The second HR rescue.

10 · 113316 resume @484.4s · on-time 22.5s

girth -6.1 s HR -11.3 s

Low-stimulation session. Girth moves only ~40 counts total but its velocity still has a clear crest. Both channels fire early; HR very early at −11.3 s.

11 · 113316 resume @593.3s · on-time 5.6s

girth -1.7 s HR +5.7 s

The odd one. Both girth and HR are falling at the press — first derivatives are negative on both sides. The trigger fires 1.7 s early but for a different reason than everywhere else.

Patterns worth chasing

  • Girth's second derivative crosses zero before the first derivative rolls over. Visible in 01, 02, 05. That is an earlier landmark than the one the detector currently uses — but also a noisier one, and it was the feature that failed significance testing at n=11.
  • HR's first derivative pinning to zero is a discrete, easy event. Episodes 02, 04, 09. It is a cleaner signal than HR's rollover fraction and might be a better basis for the HR branch than what is used now.
  • Episode 06 is unwinnable and episode 11 is a different phenomenon. Exclude both when eyeballing, or they will pull you toward the wrong rule.
  • Peak girth velocity varies 50× — from 2.8 counts/s in episode 11 to 150 in episode 05. Any absolute threshold on girth velocity will not transfer; this is why the detector scales everything by each channel's own MAD.
